In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Privy Council's devolution jurisprudence is a product of judicial politics.

a devolution issue is any question which arises as to whether a legislative or executive act of the Scottish Parliament, the National Assembly for Wales or the Northern Ireland Assembly is within or outwith the powers of those institutions.

the devolution issues are those questions which arise under the devolution statutes and their associated subordinate legislation, and which concern the extent of the legislative and executive competence of the devolved institutions, and the extent of the executive competence of the Westminster Parliament.2 Footnote 1: See Scotland Act 1998, ss. 29 and 57; Government of Wales Act 1998 (‘GWA’) s. 109; Northern Ireland Act 1998 s. 98.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the Privy Council's approach to be one of a cautious and incremental development of the law, and that the approach has been to take a broad view of devolution issues.
we have found that the devolution statutes are not the only legal sources for devolution issues.

we have been able to show that the Judicial Committee has been a significant player in the process of devolution, that its decisions have been important to the development of devolution, and that its role in the process of constitutional change has been a significant one, and that the Judicial Committee's decisions have been important in shaping the development of devolved government.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the devolution jurisprudence of the PC is a complex and evolving body of law.

, while the Supreme Court has not yet had a major opportunity to address the devolution issue, it has already begun to develop a distinctive approach to devolution cases that will likely shape the way it approaches such cases in the future.
